Basic Electricity.intro: Electric current is the flow of charge. Understanding the basic concepts of voltage, current and resistance is essential for all of P2.

sections.title: Current, Voltage and Resistance
points: Current (I) — rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes (A)
Voltage/potential difference (V) — energy transferred per unit charge; measured in volts (V)
Resistance (R) — opposition to current flow; measured in ohms (Ω)

sections.title: Ohm's Law

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance). Rearranged: I = V/R and R = V/I. An ohmic conductor has constant resistance.

points: Ohmic conductor: resistance stays constant at constant temperature (e.g. resistor)
Non-ohmic: resistance changes (e.g. filament bulb — gets hotter, resistance increases; diode — only conducts in one direction)

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Q = I × t (Charge = Current × Time). Charge is measured in coulombs (C).

keyTerms.def: The rate of flow of electric charge — measured in amperes (A)
The energy transferred per unit charge — measured in volts (V)
Opposition to current flow — measured in ohms (Ω)
V = IR — voltage, current and resistance are proportionally related in ohmic conductors

examTips: V = IR is the most used formula in electricity. Learn the triangle.
Ohmic conductors have constant resistance. Filament bulbs and diodes do not.
Charge = current × time. Charge is in coulombs (C).
commonMistakes: Confusing current (flow of charge) with voltage (energy per charge).
Saying current is 'used up' in a circuit — current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
clozePassages: Electric current is the flow of charge through a circuit, measured in amperes (A). Potential difference (voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts (V). Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). These three quantities are related by Ohm's Law: V = IR. Increasing resistance reduces current for a given potential difference.

Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature remains constant. A component that obeys Ohm's Law is called an ohmic conductor. The relationship V = IR can be rearranged to find any of the three quantities. A graph of current against voltage for an ohmic conductor gives a straight line through the origin, with gradient equal to 1/resistance.

Charge flow in a circuit is measured in coulombs (C). The relationship between charge, current and time is: Q = It. One coulomb is the charge transferred when one ampere flows for one second. In metallic conductors, electric current is carried by electrons moving through the metal lattice. Conventional current flows from positive to negative, which is opposite to the direction of electron flow.

Circuits.intro: Electrical circuits can be arranged in series or parallel. Each arrangement has different rules for current, voltage and resistance.

sections.title: Series Circuits
points: Components connected in a single loop
Same current flows through all components
Voltages add up to total voltage: Vtotal = V₁ + V₂
Resistances add up: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂
If one component breaks — circuit breaks; all go off

sections.title: Parallel Circuits
points: Components connected in separate branches
Same voltage across all branches
Currents split between branches; add up to total: Itotal = I₁ + I₂
Total resistance LESS than smallest individual resistance
If one branch breaks — others still work

sections.title: Circuit Symbols
points: Cell, battery, switch, resistor, variable resistor, lamp
Ammeter — in series; voltmeter — in parallel
Diode, LED, thermistor, LDR

keyTerms.def: Circuit where components are connected in a single loop — same current throughout
Circuit where components are on separate branches — same voltage across each branch
Instrument measuring current — connected in series
Instrument measuring potential difference — connected in parallel

examTips: Series: same current, voltages add. Parallel: same voltage, currents add.
Ammeter = series (low resistance). Voltmeter = parallel (high resistance).
Adding more parallel branches reduces total resistance.
commonMistakes: Saying voltages are the same in series — they're the same in PARALLEL.
Connecting ammeter in parallel or voltmeter in series — this is wrong.
clozePassages: In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop. The same current flows through all components. The total resistance is the sum of individual resistances. The total potential difference is shared between components. If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops working. In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. The potential difference across each branch is the same. The total current is the sum of branch currents.

Ammeters measure current and are always connected in series in a circuit. Voltmeters measure potential difference and are always connected in parallel across a component. Ammeters have very low resistance to avoid affecting the circuit. Voltmeters have very high resistance so they draw minimal current. These instruments allow the electrical quantities in a circuit to be measured accurately.

The total resistance of components in series is found by adding individual resistances: R = R₁ + R₂. For parallel circuits, the total resistance is lower than any individual resistance. Adding more components in parallel provides more paths for current, decreasing total resistance. Most household circuits are wired in parallel so that each appliance receives the full mains voltage and can be switched independently.

Domestic Electricity.intro: Mains electricity in the UK is alternating current (AC) at 230V and 50Hz. Understanding how it is safely used in the home is required for P2.

sections.title: AC vs DC
points: AC (alternating current) — direction of current reverses periodically; mains supply (230V, 50Hz UK)
DC (direct current) — current flows in one direction only; batteries and phone chargers

sections.title: The Three-Pin Plug
points: Live (brown) — carries current at 230V
Neutral (blue) — completes circuit at 0V
Earth (green/yellow) — safety wire; prevents shock if appliance develops fault
Fuse in live wire — melts if current too high, breaking circuit

sections.title: Fuses and Circuit Breakers
points: Fuse: thin wire that melts if current exceeds rating — breaks circuit
Circuit breaker: electronic switch that trips if current too high — can be reset
Choose fuse rating just above normal operating current
RCD (residual current device): detects difference in current in live and neutral — trips if earth fault

keyTerms.def: Current that reverses direction periodically — mains supply
Current that flows in one direction only — batteries
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit if current is too high
Safety wire that provides a low-resistance path to earth if appliance develops a fault

examTips: Live = brown, Neutral = blue, Earth = green/yellow. Learn the colours.
Earth wire prevents shock — if live wire touches metal casing, current flows to earth through earth wire, blowing the fuse.
AC frequency in UK = 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second).
commonMistakes: Saying neutral wire carries current at high voltage — neutral is at 0V.
Forgetting the earth wire's function — it is a safety device, not needed for the circuit to work.
clozePassages: Alternating current (AC) constantly changes direction. UK mains electricity is AC at 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only and is produced by batteries and cells. The live wire in a plug is brown and carries the alternating voltage. The neutral wire is blue and completes the circuit. The earth wire is green-yellow and is a safety wire to prevent electric shocks.

A three-pin plug connects appliances safely to the mains. The fuse is in series with the live wire and melts if the current becomes too high, breaking the circuit and preventing fire or damage. The earth wire connects the metal case of an appliance to the ground — if a fault causes the case to become live, current flows to earth and blows the fuse. Circuit breakers perform the same function but can be reset rather than replaced.

Fuses and circuit breakers are safety devices that protect circuits from excessive current. A fuse contains a thin wire that melts if the current exceeds its rated value. A circuit breaker contains a switch that trips automatically. Both break the circuit to prevent overheating and fire. The correct fuse rating should be slightly above the normal operating current of the appliance. Residual current devices (RCDs) offer additional protection against electric shock.

Power and Energy.intro: Power is the rate of energy transfer. Electrical power depends on both current and voltage.

callout.label: Formulae
callout.text: P = I × V (Power = Current × Voltage). Also: P = I² × R and P = V²/R. Power in watts (W).

sections.title: Energy Transfer

callout.label: Energy Formula
callout.text: E = P × t (Energy = Power × Time). Energy in joules (J) when time in seconds. E = Q × V (Energy = Charge × Voltage).

points: Kilowatt-hour (kWh) = energy unit used in electricity bills
Cost = power (kW) × time (hours) × price per kWh

keyTerms.def: Rate of energy transfer — measured in watts (W)
Unit of power = 1 joule per second
Unit of energy used in electricity billing = 3.6 MJ

examTips: P = IV is the most important power formula. Also know P = I²R for when V is not given.
For electricity bills: use kW and hours; multiply by cost per kWh.
commonMistakes: Using watts instead of kilowatts in electricity cost calculations.
clozePassages: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W). It can be calculated as P = E/t (energy divided by time) or P = IV (current × potential difference). One watt equals one joule per second. A 60 W light bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second. The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the unit of energy used by electricity companies — it equals the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour.

The energy transferred by an electrical appliance can be calculated using E = Pt (power × time) or E = IVt (current × voltage × time). The cost of electricity is calculated by multiplying the number of kilowatt-hours by the price per kWh. Choosing energy-efficient appliances with lower power ratings reduces electricity bills and carbon emissions. The energy rating label on appliances helps consumers compare efficiency.

Electrical power in a resistor can be calculated using P = I²R or P = V²/R. These equations are derived from combining P = IV with V = IR. Appliances with high resistance generate more heat when the same current flows through them. This is the principle behind electric heaters and toasters. In power transmission, using high voltage reduces current, which reduces the power lost as heat in the cables (P = I²R).

Static Electricity.intro: Static electricity is the build-up of electrical charge on insulating materials. It occurs when electrons are transferred by friction.

sections.title: Charging by Friction
points: When two insulators are rubbed together, electrons are transferred
Object gaining electrons becomes negatively charged
Object losing electrons becomes positively charged
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract

sections.title: Electric Fields
points: A charged object creates an electric field around it
Electric field lines point from positive to negative
A charged object in an electric field experiences a force

sections.title: Uses and Hazards
points: Uses: photocopiers, inkjet printers, paint sprayers, defibrillators
Hazards: sparks from fuel tankers (earth the tanker); risk of electric shock from large static charges
Lightning conductors: provide safe path for charge to earth

keyTerms.def: Electrical charge that builds up on insulating materials — does not flow
The region around a charged object where forces act on other charges
Connecting a charged object to earth to safely discharge it

examTips: Only electrons move when charging by friction — protons stay in the nucleus.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract — apply this in all static questions.
commonMistakes: Saying protons move during friction charging — only electrons are transferred.
Confusing static electricity (no flow) with current electricity (continuous flow).
clozePassages: Static electricity builds up when certain materials are rubbed together, causing electrons to be transferred from one material to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the one that loses electrons becomes positively charged. Like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract. Static electricity can cause sparks, which is a hazard near flammable materials.

An electric field exists around any charged object. A second charged object in this field experiences a force. The field is strongest near the object and weaker further away. Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge. Electric fields between parallel plates are uniform. Lightning occurs when the electric field between clouds and the ground is strong enough to cause a large discharge of charge through the air.

Static electricity has many practical uses. In electrostatic spray painting, charged droplets are attracted to the earthed object being painted, giving even coverage and reducing waste. Photocopiers use electrostatic attraction to transfer toner powder to paper. Defibrillators deliver a controlled electric shock to restart a stopped heart. Earthing provides a safe path for charge to flow to the ground, preventing dangerous build-up of static charge.
